strengths: Novel and well-motivated formulation: the paper is the first to cast the entire pretext pre-training / downstream fine-tuning pipeline as a joint bilevel optimization problem, rather than applying BLO only within one stage or to a specific task type as prior work does.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper derives the implicit gradient explicitly under stated convexity/differentiability assumptions, explains the role of the regularization weight λ, and gives an interpretable limiting-case analysis (large/small λ reducing to conventional fine-tuning or linear probing).

Broad empirical evaluation across 14 diverse downstream classification datasets with 10 random seeds per configuration and reported means/std, plus a dedicated experiment varying total pretraining epochs to show the improvement is not just an artifact of the pretext training budget.

Qualitative t-SNE analysis of backbone features provides complementary, non-accuracy-based evidence that BiSSL produces more class-separated downstream representations, including on datasets where accuracy gains are marginal.
Clear presentation of the training algorithm, pipeline (Fig. 1), and reproducibility details (hyperparameter tables, CG implementation details in appendix), with code and pretrained weights released.
weaknesses: Limited scale and generality: experiments use only one backbone (ResNet-18), one pretext method (SimCLR), and one pretraining dataset (STL10U); scalability to larger backbones, other SSL objectives (e.g., non-contrastive), or larger pretraining corpora is untested and left entirely to future work, which limits confidence that the reported gains transfer to realistic large-scale SSL settings.

Modest and inconsistent gains: many improvements in Table 1 are small (often <1%), several datasets show negative deltas (e.g., STL10L top-1, CIFAR100 top-1), and the criterion used to bold results as "significantly different" is not clearly specified (no explicit statistical test described), making it hard to judge the practical significance of the reported improvements.

No comparison against other backbone-priming baselines discussed in related work (COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE, MetaMask, etc.); the only baseline is the conventional "Only FT" pipeline, so it remains unclear whether BiSSL's benefits are competitive with or complementary to existing simpler priming techniques.

Computational overhead is not quantified: BiSSL requires an additional intermediate training stage with CG-based Hessian-vector product approximations, extra warm-up stages, and additional hyperparameters (λ, γ, Na, α, NU, NL, T), but no wall-clock time, memory, or FLOPs comparison to the baseline pipeline is provided to assess the cost-benefit tradeoff.

Hyperparameter selection appears heavily manual/dataset-specific (e.g., per-dataset learning rates and weight decays for warm-up and upper-level stages in Appendix Table 3, with ad hoc adjustments noted as needed based on "preliminary testing"), raising concerns about reproducibility and the risk of favorable tuning bias relative to the baseline.

The stationarity/convexity assumptions required to justify the explicit implicit-gradient formula (Section A.1) are strong and only approximately met in practice (e.g., via λ-scaling to "effectively convexify" a non-convex deep network loss), yet the paper does not empirically verify how well these assumptions hold or how sensitive results are to their violation.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel formulation of the SSL pretrain-finetune pipeline as a bilevel optimization problem, explicitly coupling pretext and downstream objectives rather than treating them as disjoint stages.

Provides a fairly rigorous derivation of the implicit gradient under stated convexity/stationarity assumptions, and a practical algorithm using CG-based Hessian-vector approximation, building sensibly on prior BLO/meta-learning techniques (Rajeswaran et al.).
Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across 14 diverse downstream image classification datasets (fine-grained, scene, texture, etc.), with results reported as mean ± std over 10 seeds.
Additional ablation over varying pretext pretraining duration and qualitative t-SNE inspection of backbone features add some insight into why/when the method may help.
Code and pretrained weights reportedly released, aiding reproducibility of the specific reported setup.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single backbone (ResNet-18), single pretext method (SimCLR), and single pretraining dataset (STL10-U), which is small-scale; despite claims of general applicability across SSL methods/modalities (also mentioned in intro/related work for audio and NLP), no such generalization is empirically tested, leaving the central claims of broad applicability unsupported.

Reported gains are frequently marginal (many <1-2 points, several negative, e.g., STL10L top-1 decreases, CIFAR100 top-1 decreases) and given overlapping/near-overlapping standard deviations for several datasets, the practical significance of the 'consistently improved or competitive' claim is weak; the criterion used to mark results as 'significantly different' in Table 1 is not clearly specified (no formal statistical test described).

No empirical comparison against the related backbone-priming baselines explicitly discussed in Section 2 (COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE, Spin) or against simpler/cheaper alternatives, making it impossible to assess whether the added complexity of full bilevel optimization is actually necessary to achieve the observed gains.

No analysis of computational overhead (wall-clock time, memory, FLOPs) of the BiSSL stage (CG iterations, extra warm-up stages, alternating optimization) relative to the modest accuracy gains, which is important for judging the cost-benefit tradeoff of adopting this fairly complex framework.

Extensive per-dataset hyperparameter search (200 random configs) is applied to both baseline fine-tuning and BiSSL fine-tuning, but the downstream head warm-up and upper-level learning rates/weight decays are manually adjusted ad hoc ('as needed when preliminary testing indicated...'), raising concerns about fair comparison and potential tuning asymmetries favoring BiSSL.

The theoretical justification relies on assuming a fixed projection head and an effectively convexified lower-level objective via large regularization weight λ, which is a strong idealization for deep non-convex networks; the paper acknowledges but does not empirically probe how badly these assumptions are violated in practice.

The qualitative t-SNE feature analysis, while illustrative, is inherently subjective and not quantified (e.g., no clustering metrics like silhouette score or linear probe accuracy on frozen features), limiting its evidentiary value for the claim of improved feature alignment.

strengths: The core idea of casting pretext pre-training and downstream fine-tuning as a bilevel optimization problem is novel and well-motivated; the paper clearly differentiates this formulation from prior BLO applications in SSL (which target sub-components like projection heads or auxiliary models) and from BLO in meta-learning (Appendix A.2), giving a clear picture of the contribution's originality.

The derivation of the implicit gradient (Section 3.3, Appendix A.1) is carried out carefully with explicit statement of the assumptions (convexified lower level, invertible Hessian) needed to justify the closed-form IG expression, and the interpretation of the regularization weight λ's effect on the algorithm's behavior (reducing to fine-tuning vs. probing in the limits) gives useful intuition.

The empirical evaluation spans 14 diverse downstream classification datasets with 10 independent seeds per configuration and reports means/standard deviations, and results show consistent non-negative or significant positive changes on most datasets without a single significant degradation, which is a reasonably strong and comprehensive evidence base for the practical benefit.

Additional analyses—performance across varying pretraining durations (Fig. 2) and t-SNE visualizations of backbone features before fine-tuning (Fig. 3 and Appendix C)—provide complementary qualitative and quantitative support for the claimed mechanism (better alignment of pretext features to downstream semantics), rather than relying on accuracy numbers alone.

The paper is transparent about implementation details (extensive hyperparameter tables in the appendix, detailed algorithm boxes, CG approximation details) and states that code and pretrained weights are publicly released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single backbone (ResNet-18), a single SSL method (SimCLR), and a single pre-training dataset (STL10-U); the paper explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about scaling to larger backbones/datasets, which limits confidence that the reported benefits generalize to the settings (large-scale pretraining, transformer backbones) where SSL is most commonly used in practice today.

The magnitude of improvement is often small and inconsistent: several datasets show a decrease in top-1 or top-5 accuracy (e.g., STL10L top-1, Flowers top-5, Aircrafts top-5, CIFAR100 top-1), and the paper's criterion for claiming a win ('significant improvement in either top-1 OR top-5') is a fairly permissive bar that could overstate the overall consistency of the gains.

No empirical comparison to the other 'backbone priming' baselines discussed in Related Work (COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE) or to other pretext-task BLO approaches (e.g., Gupta et al. 2022) is provided, making it hard to judge whether BiSSL's benefit is competitive with or superior to simpler/cheaper alternatives that address the same misalignment problem.

The additional computational cost of BiSSL (extra intermediate training stage with per-step conjugate-gradient Hessian-vector products) is not quantified in wall-clock time or FLOPs relative to the baseline pipeline, making it difficult to assess the practical cost-benefit trade-off of adopting the method.

Key hyperparameters specific to BiSSL (λ, γ, Na, α, CG iterations/damping) appear to be selected via limited informal exploration ('early experiments,' 'empirically shown to improve stability') rather than systematic ablation, so it is unclear how sensitive the method's benefits are to these choices or how a practitioner should tune them for a new setting.

The theoretical justification for the closed-form implicit gradient relies on convexifying the lower level via sufficiently large λ, yet the actual experiments use a very small λ=0.001, which the paper itself notes drives the setup toward conventional independent pretext training; this creates some tension between the theoretical motivation and the practical algorithm actually evaluated.

strengths: Proposes a genuinely novel formulation that connects pretext pre-training and downstream fine-tuning through a single bilevel optimization problem, in contrast to prior BLO-for-SSL works that only integrate BLO into one stage (pretraining or fine-tuning) and are tied to specific tasks.

Provides a clear derivation of the implicit gradient with explicit statement of the assumptions required (convexity via regularization, invertibility of Hessian, stationarity condition), and discusses interpretable limiting behavior of the regularization weight λ.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 12 diverse downstream classification datasets and two pretext methods (SimCLR, BYOL), plus an object detection task (Faster-RCNN/VOC), showing consistent (though variable) gains.
Includes a useful ablation varying pre-training duration, showing BiSSL's benefit is not simply a function of extra compute but appears related to information sharing between stages.

Qualitative t-SNE visualizations offer supporting (if informal) evidence that BiSSL produces more separable, task-aligned features prior to fine-tuning, including on datasets where accuracy gains were small.
Reasonably rigorous evaluation protocol: separate validation-based hyperparameter search, multiple random seeds, and reporting of variances, which aids credibility of the comparison.
Code and pretrained weights are stated to be made publicly available, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments use reduced image resolution (96x96 instead of the standard 224x224) and non-standard augmentation ranges, making it unclear how results relate to widely reported SimCLR/BYOL benchmarks and potentially limiting generalizability of conclusions to standard-resolution SSL pipelines.

Backbone diversity is limited to ResNet-50 (and ResNet-18 in the smaller ablation); no experiments with Vision Transformers or other architectures that dominate current SSL research, despite the method being framed as broadly applicable.

The added computational and memory overhead of BiSSL (extra warm-up stage, conjugate-gradient Hessian-vector products, storing/duplicating backbone parameters for both levels) is not quantified in wall-clock time or memory, only approximated in "equivalent epochs," making practical cost-benefit assessment difficult.

Downstream head warm-up and upper-level hyperparameters were manually adjusted "based on preliminary testing" for BiSSL, whereas baseline hyperparameters came from a fixed grid search; this asymmetry in tuning effort raises fairness concerns for the comparison.

No sensitivity analysis of the key regularization weight λ (fixed at 0.001 from unspecified "early experiments") is provided, despite the paper's own analysis showing λ critically controls the behavior of the method (interpolating between naive fine-tuning and naive pretext training).

Missing empirical comparison against the other backbone-priming baselines discussed in Related Work (COIN, RIFLE, Noisy-Tune), which would help contextualize how much of the improvement is attributable specifically to the bilevel formulation versus simpler intermediate-stage interventions.

The magnitude of improvement varies widely across datasets (e.g., near-zero on Cars/VOC07 vs. +9.6 on CUB200) without deeper analysis or hypothesis for why certain downstream distributions benefit more, limiting insight into when the method is expected to help.

The criterion for marking results as "significantly higher" in Table 1 is not clearly specified (no explicit statistical test, e.g., t-test with reported p-values), reducing confidence in the stated significance claims.

The implicit gradient derivation assumes ϕP fixed, a simplification acknowledged but not fully reconciled with the actual algorithm, which updates ϕP jointly; the theoretical guarantees are therefore only approximately applicable to the implemented method.

strengths: The core idea of framing pretext pre-training and downstream fine-tuning as a bilevel optimization problem, with an explicit regularizer linking upper- and lower-level backbone parameters, is a clean and reasonably novel way to address the pretrain/fine-tune misalignment problem, distinguishing it from prior BLO-in-SSL works that only address one stage.

The paper provides a full derivation of the implicit gradient under stated assumptions (Appendix A.1), and clearly explains the role of the regularization weight λ, connecting BiSSL to conventional fine-tuning and probing as limiting cases.

Experiments span two pretext methods (SimCLR, BYOL), 12 downstream classification datasets, and an object detection task, showing broadly consistent, often large, gains (e.g., +9.6 on CUB200 with SimCLR) with lower variance than baseline.

Additional analyses (pretraining-duration sweep, t-SNE visualizations of lower-level backbone features) attempt to substantiate the central claim that BiSSL improves feature alignment prior to fine-tuning, not just final accuracy.
The training algorithm is presented as task-agnostic and the authors release code and pretrained weights, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: No empirical comparison against the other 'priming pre-trained backbones' baselines discussed in Related Work (COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE) or the other BLO-based SSL methods (LoGo, OSSL, MetaMask, BLO-SAM), so it is unclear whether the gains stem specifically from the bilevel formulation versus simpler alternative interventions between pre-training and fine-tuning.

The pretext image resolution is reduced to 96x96 (versus the standard 224x224 used in the cited SimCLR/BYOL/VICReg setups), a substantial deviation from standard practice that is not well justified and complicates comparison to the broader SSL literature and to the reported baseline accuracies of these methods elsewhere.

No wall-clock time, memory, or FLOPs comparison is provided for the additional CG-based bilevel training stage versus standard fine-tuning, despite the paper acknowledging CG's computational overhead; the claim that BiSSL adds 'negligible' epochs (≈8 of 500) ignores that CG requires multiple Hessian-vector products per step, which likely dominates wall-clock cost.

Downstream evaluation is restricted to a single linear layer for classification (linear probing/fine-tuning of a linear head), leaving open whether the reported benefits persist for more complex downstream heads or full end-to-end fine-tuning architectures beyond the single Faster-RCNN detection experiment.

The regularization weight λ and other BiSSL-specific hyperparameters (NL, NU, T) appear to have been selected via limited informal 'early experiments' rather than systematic ablation, raising concerns about sensitivity and the fairness of the hyperparameter search budget relative to the baseline (100 random configs) versus BiSSL variants.

Quantitative feature-alignment evidence is entirely qualitative (t-SNE plots); no quantitative alignment metric (e.g., kNN accuracy, linear probe accuracy on frozen lower-level features, silhouette score) is reported to substantiate the alignment claim beyond visual inspection.

Some datasets show negligible or no improvement (e.g., Cars for SimCLR shows 0.0 average difference), and the paper does not analyze what dataset properties predict when BiSSL helps versus not, limiting the generalizability claims.

The Impact Statement / limitations discussion is minimal and does not address the added computational/environmental cost of an extra bilevel training stage with second-order gradient approximations, which seems relevant given the stated cost concerns raised by the authors themselves in Section 3.3.

strengths: The core idea of framing pretext pre-training and downstream fine-tuning as a bilevel optimization problem is well-motivated and clearly differentiated from prior BLO-in-SSL work (Gupta et al., LoGo, OSSL, MetaMask, BLO-SAM), which apply BLO within a single stage rather than jointly across pretext and downstream stages.

The theoretical derivation of the implicit gradient is carried out carefully, with explicit statement of the assumptions required (convexified lower-level objective via regularization, fixed pretext head, invertible Hessian) and a full derivation provided in the appendix, which aids transparency about the method's limits.

The empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive: two pretext methods (SimCLR, BYOL), 12 diverse downstream classification datasets, an object detection task (Faster-RCNN on VOC07+12), a pre-training-duration ablation, and qualitative t-SNE feature visualizations, all pointing in a consistent direction.

BiSSL improves accuracy on 10/12 datasets with no observed regressions and generally lower variance than the baseline, and the additional compute overhead of the BiSSL stage is modest (~8 extra pretext-equivalent epochs relative to 500 epochs of pre-training).

Reproducibility is well supported by an extensive appendix documenting hyperparameters (learning rates, weight decays) for every dataset and training stage, as well as algorithmic/implementation details of the conjugate-gradient Hessian-vector product computation.
weaknesses: All main experiments use a single architecture (ResNet-50) and only two closely related pretext methods (SimCLR, BYOL); no evidence is given that the approach transfers to other backbone families (e.g., ViTs) or to non-contrastive/non-BYOL-style pretext objectives, limiting claims of general applicability despite the paper's framing as "task-agnostic".

The paper does not empirically compare BiSSL against the other backbone-priming baselines it explicitly discusses in related work (COIN, Noisy-Tune, RIFLE), so it is unclear whether BiSSL's gains are meaningfully larger than simpler, cheaper alternatives that also modify the backbone between pre-training and fine-tuning.

Only one instantiation of the regularization function r (squared L2 distance) is evaluated, even though the framework is presented as accommodating any convex r; the sensitivity of results to this choice, and to the key hyperparameter λ, is not systematically studied beyond a brief qualitative remark.

Several hyperparameters (e.g., downstream head warm-up learning rates) were manually adjusted based on "preliminary testing indicating potential for improved convergence," which is not a fully specified or reproducible procedure and raises minor concerns about equal tuning effort being given to baseline vs. BiSSL pipelines.

The pre-training-duration ablation (Section 4.3.2), which is important for supporting generality claims, is conducted with a smaller-scale ResNet-18/STL-10 setup rather than the main ImageNet/ResNet-50 configuration, and is limited to a single downstream dataset (Flowers), making it a weaker piece of evidence than the main results.

The paper does not report wall-clock training time or additional GPU-memory overhead of the CG-based implicit gradient computation, only an epoch-equivalent estimate, making it harder for practitioners to judge the real-world practicality of adopting BiSSL.

Statistical significance testing methodology behind the bolding of "significantly higher" results is not explicitly described (e.g., which test, threshold), which slightly weakens the rigor of the comparative claims.
